  "brief": "The evidence supports documented production failure modes for OT in Etherpad and ShareDB/ot.js (concurrent-delete transform bugs, reconnect/pending-op state errors, revision-store corruption — symptom: replica divergence or silently dropped edits [s29][s26][s25][s18]) and for CRDTs in Yjs and Automerge (rich-text binding data loss, sync-protocol non-convergence, memory leaks, undo/GC corruption — including reports of production data loss [s47][s32][s92][s91][s60]).   "report": "## 1. What the evidence actually covers (and what it does not)\n\nThe question names four illustrative systems: Google Docs, Etherpad-style servers, Figma, and \"comparable deployed tools.\" The evidence does not cover all four equally, and one is not covered at all.\n\n- **Figma**: no source in the provided list discusses Figma's editing engine, its internals, or any documented failure mode. The question's mention of Figma is not supported by any evidence here. Anything said about Figma specifically would be unsupported and is omitted.\n- **Google Docs**: most sources about Google Docs are third-party \"system design\" tutorials and blog posts that *reconstruct* a presumed OT architecture for interview-prep or educational purposes [s9][s12][s13][s76][s84][s85][s89]. These are not primary engineering documentation from Google and should not be read as confirmed internal implementation detail. Two sources describe user-facing symptoms rather than architecture: an official Google support troubleshooting page for \"not saving / edits not appearing\" [s86], and a third-party diagnostic write-up on the same symptom class [s81]. These establish that such symptoms are *documented as user-facing problems*, but not their root cause inside Google's stack.\n- **Etherpad**: genuinely covered by primary evidence — its own GitHub issue tracker and official documentation describe its OT-based changeset architecture and specific bugs [s16][s18][s19][s23][s26][s27][s77]–[s83][s87].\n- **ShareDB / ot.js / json0**: covered by primary GitHub sources for a real, deployed OT library stack (used to build collaborative apps), including specific bug reports [s20]–[s22][s24][s25][s28]–[s30].\n- **Yjs / y-prosemirror / y-codemirror / y-crdt**: covered by primary GitHub issue trackers, official docs, and a community forum report explicitly describing a **production** data-loss incident [s31][s32][s36][s38]–[s60].\n- **Automerge**: covered by primary GitHub issue trackers [s90]–[s101].\n- **Academic OT/CRDT papers** [s1]–[s8][s10][s11][s14][s15][s61]–[s75] are theoretical/algorithmic treatments and comparative surveys, not reports of production incidents. They are useful for root-cause vocabulary and for the theoretical OT-vs-CRDT debate, not as evidence of what actually broke in a deployed system.\n\nBecause of this, the report below documents failure modes with **medium-to-good confidence for Etherpad and for Yjs/Automerge**, and with **low confidence for anything specific to Google Docs**, and **no evidence at all for Figma**.\n\n## 2. OT: documented practical failure modes\n\nEtherpad's model — browser sends changesets, server relays and stores them as revision history — is documented in its own architecture docs [s77][s87].\n\n- **Incorrect transform for concurrent deletes at the same position.** ot.js issue #30 reports a reproducible \"out of sync\" state when two clients delete at the same cursor position, with the maintainers identifying a transform-rule defect [s29]. Root cause: an asymmetric/incomplete transform rule. Symptom: two clients end with different document contents from operations that should be equivalent. Severity: critical — this is direct replica divergence.\n- **Pending local edits not retransmitted after reconnect.** Etherpad issue #5108 reports that a reconnecting client renders optimistic local edits but does not resend the pending changeset until a further edit occurs, producing visibly different text between users (one client shows a shorter/older version) [s26]. Root cause: client reconnect/transport state machine, not the transform algebra itself. Severity: high, and can become data loss for the reconnecting user if the pending edit is never resent.\n- **JSON OT type loses concurrent structural edits on convergence.** The ShareDB `json0` status discussion is cited as noting that this OT type can lose concurrent edits [s25]. Root cause: inadequate operation semantics for concurrent structural/move operations. Symptom: replicas agree, but on a result that silently omits one user's accepted operation — a different failure shape from divergence. Severity: high (intent-preservation failure without visible disagreement between clients).\n- **Reconnect instability short of full divergence.** Etherpad issue #3078 documents a client stuck in a repeating \"reconnecting… connected\" cycle [s16], and issue #3613 documents a JSON-protocol error accompanied by a server shutdown [s19]. Root cause: transport/session layer rather than the transform rules. Severity: primarily availability, but can block editing indefinitely.\n- **Persistence/revision-store corruption independent of the transform layer.** Etherpad issue #5137 reports a pad being overwritten while old revisions remained in the database [s18], and issue #1653 discusses sanitizing a corrupted pad by rewriting all database entries [s23]. Root cause: storage/head-pointer state, not OT correctness. Severity: potentially catastrophic (users see stale/default content) but sometimes recoverable because history is retained.\n\n**Characteristic OT pattern**: the same operation stream is applied, but different replicas transform or apply it differently, producing divergence, silently lost edits, or misapplied operations. A central sequencing server (as Etherpad and ShareDB use) reduces exposure to some of these failures but does not make transform-rule bugs, reconnect logic, or storage handling safe by itself.\n\n## 3. CRDT: documented practical failure modes\n\nYjs's shared types are designed to converge without OT-style transformation [s31][s40].\n\n- **Rich-text binding deletes the object future edits depend on.** y-prosemirror issue #108 is filed as a \"[Major bug] data loss in collaborative scenario\": deleting a ProseMirror node also destroyed the underlying `Y.Text` object it was bound to, so later changes addressed to that object were lost, with reported frequent loss in collaborative table editing [s47]. Root cause: editor-binding/model-mapping logic, not the core CRDT merge law. Severity: critical content loss, but localized to the binding layer.\n- **Reported production data loss with no undo record.** A Yjs community forum post titled \"Random, rare data loss in production with y-prosemirror\" reports paragraphs disappearing during normal editing, not recoverable via reload, and absent even from snapshots — implying the content was removed from the shared document itself, not merely hidden in the UI [s32]. This is one of the strongest pieces of evidence that CRDT convergence does not guarantee no data is ever lost. Severity: critical.\n- **Local persistence failure silently stops future edits from reaching the CRDT.** Yjs issue #650 reports that `y-indexeddb` can throw when its underlying connection closes, and that this exception can unmount the editor's update plugin, so subsequent keystrokes are typed but never reach the shared document [s51]. Root cause: persistence-provider/editor-binding integration. Severity: high — the UI gives no indication that sync has stopped.\n- **Synchronization protocol failing to reach eventual consistency.** Automerge issue #870, titled \"Documents are not always eventually consistent: Synchronisation fails in specific scenarios,\" reports peers remaining in different states after synchronization [s92]. This is the CRDT analogue of OT divergence, but the fault is attributed to the sync-protocol implementation rather than the CRDT merge function. Severity: critical if confirmed as described by the issue title.
- **Problems from simultaneous multi-peer sync.** Automerge issue #536, \"Simultaneous syncing from multiple peers,\" documents complications when sync messages arrive concurrently from more than one peer [s93]. Severity: high, contingent on whether the underlying merge remains correct once messages are reconciled.\n- **Sync-message generation not tracking changes.** Automerge issue #945 reports `generateSyncMessage` failing to track changes under some conditions in a specific version [s94]. Severity: unclear from the issue title alone; flagged as a sync-layer defect distinct from merge correctness.\n- **Memory leak causing process/tab exhaustion.** Automerge issue #903 reports a memory leak associated with `initSyncState` [s91]. Symptom: growing memory use; severity: high availability risk (can force a tab/process restart, risking unsaved local state).\n- **Resource exhaustion with large/multiple documents.** Yjs issue #675 reports performance problems in `applyUpdate`/`encodeStateAsUpdate` [s55]; Automerge issue #896 reports an out-of-memory WASM error (\"unreachable at __rg_oom\") when creating multiple large documents [s97]. Severity: availability/performance, with data-loss risk if a crash precedes persistence.\n- **Undo/redo and garbage-collection interactions.** Yjs issue #204 reports that undoing deletions sometimes does not work [s57]; issue #317 reports that undo/redo can corrupt nested data structures [s60]. Root cause: interaction between the undo manager, garbage collection, and nested shared types — an application/history layer built on top of the CRDT, not the core merge algorithm. Severity: medium to high, since undo is often the user's primary recovery path after an accidental deletion.\n- **Memory not freed after document teardown.** Yjs issue #125 reports memory not being freed after `y.destroy()` [s50]. Severity: operational/availability, particularly for long-running multi-document deployments.\n\n**Characteristic CRDT pattern**: the core merge law is generally designed to converge for any valid, fully-delivered set of updates, but the surrounding system — editor bindings, persistence providers, sync-message generation, undo history, and garbage collection — is where the evidence shows practical failures occurring, up to and including outright data loss in a stated production deployment [s32][s47].\n\n## 4. Root cause, symptom, and severity: how they differ\n\n| Dimension | OT (evidence: Etherpad, ShareDB/ot.js) | CRDT (evidence: Yjs, Automerge) |\n|---|---|---|\n| Primary documented root cause | Transform-rule defects for concurrent operations at the same position/range [s29]; client reconnect/pending-operation state machine [s26]; revision-store/head corruption [s18] | Editor-binding logic that deletes the shared object a mapped node points to [s47]; persistence-provider failures that silently stop updates reaching the CRDT [s51]; sync-protocol defects preventing eventual consistency [s92][s93]; undo/GC/nested-structure interactions [s57][s60]; resource exhaustion [s55][s97][s91] |\n| Typical worst symptom in the evidence | Two replicas end up with different document contents after equivalent-looking concurrent operations, or one accepted operation is silently dropped [s29][s25] | A paragraph or node vanishes from the shared document itself, not recoverable by reload, in a stated production deployment [s32][s47] |\n| Relation between the core algorithm and correctness | A transform-rule bug directly and immediately causes divergence — the OT algorithm's correctness is load-bearing for every concurrent edit [s29] | The evidence's worst failures (s32, s47) are attributed to the binding/integration layer around the CRDT rather than to the merge law failing to converge; the sync-protocol issues (s92, s93) are closer to a direct CRDT-layer failure but are less numerous in this evidence set |\n| Recovery path documented | Reload from server-held revision history, when local pending edits survive the reconnect defect [s26]; manual DB sanitization for corrupted pads [s23] | Any healthy replica may hold the correct state, but recovery fails once the deleting binding action has already been applied and propagated [s47] |\n| Resource-related failure | Not prominent in the OT evidence provided | Recurs across multiple sources: memory leaks [s91][s50], OOM on large documents [s97], undo/GC costs [s57] |\n\n## 5. Disagreement in the evidence\n\nTwo distinct kinds of disagreement are visible.\n\n**(a) Disagreement about what \"conflict-free\" actually guarantees.** The Yjs/Automerge production reports [s32][s47][s92] show that a CRDT's deterministic-merge property does not, in practice, prevent data loss — it depends on whether all updates are correctly generated, transported, and bound to the application model. This is in some tension with framing in introductory CRDT material [s31][s40], which emphasizes conflict-free merging without qualifying it against binding/persistence/sync-layer failures. The report treats this as a real gap between the formal guarantee and the deployed behavior, not as one source being \"wrong\" — the formal guarantee and the reported bugs are about different layers of the same system.\n\n**(b) A theoretical dispute in the academic literature, not settled by this evidence.** Multiple papers by overlapping authors are titled some variant of \"Real Differences between OT and CRDT ... for/in Co-Editors,\" across several venues and versions [s62][s63][s65][s66][s69][s70][s73]. Their titles indicate an explicit argument that OT and CRDT differ in correctness and complexity for consistency maintenance — i.e., a position that the two approaches are not simply interchangeable trade-offs. The evidence available here is limited to titles/abstracts-level indication that this debate exists; the specific claims and which side prevails are **not established by what was provided**, and should not be asserted beyond \"a documented academic disagreement exists about the comparative correctness/complexity of OT versus CRDT approaches.\" Attaching a specific technical claim from these papers would be unsupported without the paper content.\n\n## 6. What remains unsettled, and what would settle it\n\n- **Figma**: entirely unaddressed. Nothing here would let a reader make any claim about Figma's failure modes; only a source describing Figma's actual sync engine and incident history would settle this.\n- **Google Docs internals**: the tutorials describing Google Docs as OT-based are third-party reconstructions [s9][s12][s13][s76][s84][s85][s89], not confirmed by Google. Official material here is limited to generic troubleshooting steps [s86] and a third-party diagnostic post [s81], neither of which confirms root cause. Only Google's own engineering documentation or a public postmortem would settle whether the failure modes above generalize to Google Docs specifically.\n- **Frequency and population-level severity**: nearly all evidence for both paradigms is individual GitHub issues, forum posts, or maintainer discussion — not aggregated incident statistics or formal postmortems. It is not established here how common any given failure mode is in production, only that it has been reported at least once. A vendor incident report, SRE postmortem, or systematic bug-tracker analysis (counting issue frequency/severity over time) would be needed to move from \"documented to occur\" to \"documented as common or rare.\"\n- **Whether CRDT sync-protocol non-convergence (s92, s93) is a core-algorithm failure or an implementation bug**: the issue titles suggest a sync-layer defect rather than a flaw in the CRDT data type itself, but the underlying diagnosis/fix detail was not available in the material provided. Access to the linked issue discussions and any subsequent fix commit would settle whether this is a transient implementation bug or a structural property of Automerge's sync protocol.\n- **The academic OT/CRDT correctness-and-complexity dispute** (s62/s63/s65/s66/s69/s70/s73): resolving this would require reading the actual argument and comparing it against a counter-claim from CRDT proponents, neither of which is available at the depth needed here.",
  "confidence": "medium"
